cues.observation: Hand-painted ceramic azulejo street plaque reading 'COSTURERA' set into the plastered corner wall - Spanish word, and the glazed-tile street-name plaque is a strongly Andalusian convention.
Spanish road signs: round white-bordered red 'no entry' disc, blue square one-way arrow, blue pedestrian-crossing square with red-bordered outline - EU/Spanish design set.

Two-storey terraced 'adosados' in cream/ochre/salmon lime-wash with Arabic barrel roof tiles, round oculus windows, small wrought-iron Juliet balconies - classic Lower Guadalquivir vernacular pastiche.
A row of mock-Tudor / 'alpine' half-timbered gables with deep eaves and green-and-red striped awnings - an odd themed 1990s-2000s urbanization typical of Seville-belt speculative housing estates.
Curved swan-neck aluminium street lamps on slim galvanised poles plus brick-paved sidewalk bands with red-painted kerb restrictions - standard Andalusian municipal kit.
Solar thermal hot-water panels on rooftops, ubiquitous split-unit air conditioners on every facade, heavy window grilles - hot-summer southern Spain rather than the wetter north.
Clipped cypress/thuja privacy hedges over brick garden walls, no grass verges, dusty street edges - dry Mediterranean lowland planting.
Four-storey red-brick 1970s-80s bloques with garage doors at street level next to newer low-rise estates and a landscaped traffic island - a growing satellite town, not a historic city core.
Street horizon is dead flat with no hills or sea in any view - consistent with the Guadalquivir plain rather than coastal Malaga/Cadiz or hilly interior.
Dense on-street parking of European compacts (Opel, Peugeot, Seat/VW) with long white EU-format plates; traffic keeps to the right.

No tourist infrastructure, no commercial frontage beyond garage doors - a purely residential commuter neighbourhood of a mid-sized Andalusian town or a satellite of a provincial capital.

Circular white-on-red 'no entry' disc with thin rim and a small square street plate on the building corner; blue circular mandatory arrow disc on a slim grey pole — DGT hardware style.

Zebra crossings of wide white bars without preceding shark-teeth, kerbs painted with yellow/ochre restriction bands, and brick-red pigmented sidewalk aprons at corners — typical Spanish municipal practice.

Two-storey terraced 'adosados' in cream and salmon lime-wash render with barrel-tile hipped roofs, small round oculus windows and wrought-iron reja grilles over ground-floor openings — the standard 1990s-2000s Sevillian/lower Guadalquivir suburban vernacular.

A row of pseudo-Alpine/'estilo tirolés' townhouses with decorative half-timbering and deep tiled eaves — a fashion found in speculative Andalusian urbanizaciones of the 1980s-90s, indicating a planned suburban extension rather than a historic core.

Clipped Cupressus/thuja hedges over brick-pillar fences, no street trees on the residential streets, parched light, dust film on facades — dry interior Guadalquivir lowland rather than humid Atlantic north Spain.
Solar thermal collector panel mounted on a flat roof terrace; almost every window has an external split-AC condenser unit — high cooling demand consistent with Seville-area summers.

Adjacent 4-storey red-brick 1970s-80s bloques with garage doors at street level and enclosed balconies, immediately abutting low terraced housing — a growth-town profile of a large satellite municipality in a metropolitan belt, not a small village.
Flat horizon at the end of every street with no mountain backdrop — rules out Granada/Malaga basins, fits the Guadalquivir plain.
Dense on-street parking of European compacts (Opel, Peugeot, Ford, Seat-class) with long-rectangular EU plates, driving on the right.

correction.summary: HIT at city level (0.74 km error): Spain / Seville province / Dos Hermanas was correctly read from the azulejo corner street tile with a bare Spanish noun ('COSTURERA'), Sevillian cream-and-salmon adosados with barrel tiles and rejas, DGT-style thin-rimmed prohibition discs, and a completely flat street-end horizon. The alternatives Portugal and Italy were correctly excluded (no 'Rua'/'Via' generic prefix, no calçada paving, no marble via-slab), and Granada/Malaga were excluded by the absence of any sierra silhouette. The exact municipality was not separable from the images; the correct pick rested on the metropolitan-satellite morphology (1970s brick bloques with street-level garages abutting a large 1990s adosado estate).

discriminators.title: Andalusian azulejo street plaque vs Portuguese enamel 'RUA' plate
discriminators.body: In Andalusia street names appear on hand-painted ceramic tiles cemented flush into the rendered corner wall, usually giving only the bare name with no generic word. In Portugal you would instead see a rectangular enamel or tiled plate that almost always begins with 'RUA/AVENIDA/LARGO', and the pavement would be calçada portuguesa limestone mosaic rather than poured concrete slabs with red-pigmented crossing aprons.

discriminators.title: Sevillian salmon-render adosados vs Levante flat-roof suburbia
discriminators.body: Around Seville and the lower Guadalquivir, 1990s terraces are lime-rendered cream/ochre with a contrasting painted skirting band, hipped barrel-tile roofs, small oculus windows and heavy wrought-iron rejas. In the Levante (Valencia/Murcia/Alicante coast) you would instead see flatter roofs or terraced azoteas, more white or pastel-blue render, palms in the street and beach-town apartment massing.

discriminators.title: Flat closed street-end horizon separates Seville plain from Granada/Malaga
discriminators.body: In the Guadalquivir lowland around Seville every long street view ends in flat hazy sky and low rooflines. In the Vega de Granada or the Malaga basin at least one street axis would frame a sierra silhouette, and hillside terracing or stepped blocks would appear on the skyline instead.

discriminators.title: Metro-satellite signature: brick bloques with garage fronts next to adosado estates
discriminators.body: Large Seville-belt satellites (Dos Hermanas, Alcala de Guadaira, Mairena) show 1970s four-storey red-brick blocks with street-level garage doors grading directly into vast uniform gated adosado estates, often including pseudo-Tyrolean half-timbered rows from speculative 80s-90s urbanizaciones. In the historic Seville core you would instead find continuous 3-4 storey facades on narrow streets with no front gardens or garage aprons, and in a genuine rural pueblo the estate uniformity and volume would be absent.

discriminators.title: Spanish kerb-and-apron colour coding vs Italian street furniture
discriminators.body: Spanish municipalities mark parking restrictions with yellow-painted kerb bands and lay brick-red pigmented concrete aprons at crossings and corners, with thin-rimmed DGT discs on slim grey poles. In Italy you would instead see blue/white/yellow painted parking bays on the carriageway, marble or stone street-name slabs on facades, and municipal fingerposts with generics like 'Impianti sportivi'.
